openings.company: Mid-sized insurer with offices on Reforma, Mexico City
openings.raw: Auto claims service executive. Takes calls from policyholders after a crash, files the report, coordinates the adjuster and the tow truck, follows up until payment. openings.title: Auto claims service executive

activities.name: Take a crash report by phone
activities.detail: The policyholder calls right after the accident. Exact facts (location, vehicles, injuries, third parties) have to be drawn out of someone who is shaken, and recorded properly so the rest of the process works.

activities.name: Hold calls with angry or frightened people
activities.detail: Many policyholders call upset. The task is to stay calm, be clear about what comes next and keep control of the conversation, call after call.

activities.name: Coordinate adjuster and tow truck in real time
activities.detail: Assign the people in the field, confirm arrival times and keep the policyholder, who is waiting on the street, informed of where each one is.

activities.name: Follow several open files until payment
activities.detail: Each case has its own status, pending documents and notices to the customer. With several cases at once, you have to know what is missing in each and who has it, until it is paid.

hard.text: Your ad says there are lots of angry customers and high turnover. Activity 02 is where you lose people, so the fields below were chosen around it.

requirements.note: None of the four activities needs it. If it is company policy it stays, but it shuts out almost everyone who works in emergency dispatch.
Coverage, deductibles and the claims file can be taught in the first weeks. Holding the call can't be taught that fast.

fields.name: Emergency dispatch (911 / C5)
fields.same: They answer calls from people in crisis, get the location and the facts with ordered questions, send units and track their arrival.
fields.teach: Coverage and deductibles, and following a file for weeks. In dispatch every case closes in minutes.
fields.find: Current and former operators at emergency call centres. Many want to get off night shifts, so the schedule matters as much as the pay.

fields.name: Airline and airport passenger service
fields.same: They deal with upset passengers when a flight is cancelled, rebook them by coordinating with ground staff, and follow the compensation claim until it is paid.
fields.teach: Taking a report by phone about something that just happened, with exact facts. Their work is almost all face to face.
fields.find: Counter and passenger service staff at the airport, especially those who want a job without 4 a.m. starts.

fields.name: Telecom customer service
fields.same: They take calls from upset customers and explain the steps of their case.
fields.teach: Nearly everything else: coordinating people in the field, taking a report and carrying a case for weeks. Worth it only if they pass the practical test.
fields.find: Phone and internet contact centres. Plenty of people are available, which is why it pays to filter with the test before interviewing.

ad.headline: When someone crashes, yours is the first voice that helps
ad.body:
When someone crashes, the first call is to us. They are nervous, sometimes angry, and they need someone to ask the right questions and tell them what happens next. That someone would be you.

Your job is to take those calls, file the report with the facts that matter (where they are, who is hurt, which vehicles are involved), send the adjuster and the tow truck, and tell the policyholder when they will arrive. After that you don't let go of the case: you carry it through documents, calls and updates until it is paid.

You will have several cases open at once, so you need order to know what comes next in each, and patience to explain the same thing clearly again.

If you have worked in emergency dispatch, in passenger service when a flight is cancelled, or in any job where you coordinate people on the move while someone needs you right now, this will feel familiar. You do not need insurance experience.

Office: [LOCATION]. Hours: [HOURS]. Pay: [PAY].

test.title: Simulated crash call
test.setup: Someone on your team plays a policyholder who has just crashed on the Periférico. They are shaken and give the information out of order. The candidate takes the call with no script.
steps: Give them two minutes to read what the report needs: location, injuries, vehicles and third parties.
Run the call for eight minutes. The caller interrupts, gets angry once and changes one fact halfway through.
Ask them to tell you, in one minute, what they recorded and what they would tell the policyholder happens next.
Compare what they recorded against what the caller said.
test.good: Asks about injuries and location first, confirms the fact that changed, does not argue when shouted at, and closes by saying what will happen and how soon.
criteria: Asked about injuries and location before anything else
Caught and confirmed the fact that changed
Did not argue when shouted at
Closed by saying what happens next and how soon

questions.q: Tell me about a time you had to get precise information from someone who was very upset or frightened. What did you ask, in what order, and what did you do when they couldn't answer?
questions.listen: A real, specific situation. Questions ordered from most urgent to secondary, tone adjusted to the person, key facts verified and a complete record. If they only talk about "being empathetic" without saying what facts they got, it is a weak answer.

questions.q: Think of a time a customer shouted at you or was very angry about something that was not your fault. What did you say and how did the conversation end?
questions.listen: They did not get defensive or argue, they acknowledged the problem, explained what they could do and closed with a clear next step. A plus if they admit what did not go well.

questions.q: Tell me about a moment when you had to coordinate several people in different places to solve something urgent. How did you know where each one was, and what did you do when someone was late?
questions.listen: How they tracked it (calls, messages, a log), how they kept the person waiting informed, and what they changed when something failed. Examples from any field count if there are people on the move and a time limit.

questions.q: Describe a period when you had several cases or tasks open at once, each at a different stage. How did you stop any of them being forgotten before it closed?
questions.listen: A concrete method (list, spreadsheet, system, daily review), how they prioritised, how they notified the people affected, and one case that nearly got stuck and how they caught it.

ad.headline: Welcome patients and families, and make the bill clear
ad.body:
We are looking for someone to receive people at a delicate moment and make sure the paperwork does not make their day harder. The job is to register each patient with their details and documents, check with the insurer that the medical policy is in force and what it covers, and gather all the charges of the stay into a clear account and its invoice. At discharge you will see relatives who arrive in a hurry or with doubts about what is being charged and what the insurance pays, and you will explain the account calmly.

If you work today at a hotel, a car rental counter, a firm that invoices, or anywhere you verify details, close accounts with many items and explain a charge to someone who is not happy, you probably already do most of this. You do not need to have worked in a hospital or an insurer; the processes and the medical terms can be learned.

Location: [LOCATION]. Hours: [HOURS]. Pay: [PAY].

test.title: Close an account and explain it
test.setup: Hand over a sheet with twelve charges from a two-day stay, coming from three areas, and a one-paragraph policy summary with a deductible and co-insurance. Everything is made up and needs no medical vocabulary.
steps: Give them ten minutes to build the account and separate what the insurer pays from what the family pays.
One of the twelve charges is duplicated. Do not mention it.
Someone on your team plays a tired relative and asks why they have to pay anything if they have insurance.
Ask the candidate to explain it in three minutes, face to face.
test.good: Finds the duplicated charge before adding up, explains deductible and co-insurance in plain words, and does not get defensive when the relative gets upset.
criteria: Found the duplicated charge before adding up
Split the insurer and family amounts correctly
Explained deductible and co-insurance in plain words
Stayed calm when the relative got upset

questions.q: Describe an account or invoice you built from charges coming from several sources or areas. How did you make sure it added up, and what did you do when you found a difference?

ad.headline: Accounting assistant: keep several clients' numbers in order, month after month
ad.body:
At an accounting firm of about 40 people in Del Valle we are looking for someone who enjoys leaving the numbers in order. The job is on site, 9 to 6. During the month you will enter journal entries in CONTPAQi for different clients and check that every debit has its credit. You will take the bank statements, compare them with the books and trace each difference, item by item, until it balances. You will also prepare the information the team needs for the monthly tax returns, with dates that do not move.

Month-end close is the most intense part: a lot of work lands in a few days and accuracy has to hold. We are telling you now, and that is why we want people who have already worked with closes, cut-offs or balancing, whether they come from a bank, a warehouse, a shop or an office. CONTPAQi can be learned; the patience to find a difference of a few pesos, not so easily.

If you studied accounting or left it halfway, we are interested too. Location: [LOCATION]. Hours: [HOURS]. Pay: [PAY].

test.title: Find the difference
test.setup: Hand over two sheets with twenty transactions each: a bank statement and the internal record for the same month. The closing balances differ by a small amount. No accounting knowledge is needed.
steps: Three differences are planted: one missing transaction, one duplicate and one with two digits swapped.
Give them twenty minutes and say when ten have passed.
Ask them to mark each difference and write in one line where it comes from.
Ask what they would do if one difference was left that they could not explain.
test.good: Works in order instead of checking at random, finds the swapped digits, and if something does not balance writes it down instead of forcing the total.
criteria: Worked through the sheets in order
Found the missing and the duplicate transaction
Wrote down what did not balance instead of forcing it

questions.q: Tell me about a time you had to enter a lot of data or documents into a system and it had to be exact. What was the volume, how did you check your work, and what happened when you found an error?
questions.listen: A concrete volume, a method of their own for checking (not just "I was careful"), a real error they caught and how they fixed it, and what changed afterwards.

questions.q: Describe a case where two records that should match (tills, stock, balances, lists) did not. How did you find where the difference came from?
questions.listen: An ordered way of tracing (narrowing by date, amount, item), the real cause they found, and what they did when part of the difference could not be explained.

questions.q: Tell me about a time you had to hand complete information to someone else before a deadline you could not move. What was missing and how did you get it?
questions.listen: A real external deadline, how they spotted what was missing in time, how they asked others for it and what they decided when something did not arrive.

questions.q: Think of the heaviest period you have had at work, with a lot concentrated in a few days. How did you organise your time and avoid mistakes from rushing?
questions.listen: A specific example with days and quantities, an order of priorities they can explain, a way of still checking under pressure, and honesty about what was hard or went wrong.

questions.q: Tell me about a system you had to learn on the job. How long did it take before you could work without asking, and how did you learn it?
questions.listen: A named system, a rough time, and a method: notes, practice on real cases, asking a specific person. Vague confidence without an example is a weak answer.
